p.x:
My name is Ploy and I'm in my last year of primary school. I go to school by bus with my bag full of books. My classroom has thirty desks, and I sit next to my best friend, Fah.
Our first lesson starts at 8:30. We study Thai, maths, science and English. My English teacher, Mr Ben, is from Australia. He is very funny and teaches us songs. In maths, we use a ruler and a notebook every day. I often forget my eraser, so Fah lends me hers!
At 10:00 we have a break, and at 12:00 we eat lunch in the canteen. After school, I play football with my friends. Next term I will start secondary school. I am a little nervous, but my mum says I am clever and will be fine.

In Thailand, students who finish secondary school have several choices. Some have already studied at a boarding school, but most have lived at home. Many go to university to study for a degree. To get a place, they usually take entrance exams, and many students study with a tutor in the evenings and at weekends to prepare.
University life is very different from school. Most students live in a dormitory on campus for the first year, and they must manage their own time. A university year is divided into two semesters, and there are fewer rules about attendance.
However, university is not the only way. Some students enrol in vocational colleges, where they learn practical skills like engineering, cooking or hotel work. After two or three years, they receive a diploma or a certificate. Employers often say these graduates are ready to work immediately.
The best choice depends on the student. As one teacher explains, "The important thing is to find something that motivates you."

p.t: What Makes a Good Education System?
p.x:
Every few years, international rankings compare education systems, and countries such as Finland and Singapore regularly appear near the top. Interestingly, these two countries take very different approaches.
Singapore is known for a rigorous curriculum, high expectations and frequent standardised tests. Discipline is strict, and students spend long hours studying. Critics argue that this system encourages rote learning, but supporters point out that students develop excellent literacy and maths skills.
Finland, by contrast, starts formal schooling late, at the age of seven; before that, children attend kindergarten, where they learn mainly through play. There are few national exams, and assessment is mostly done by teachers, who are highly trained and trusted. Schools also offer many extracurricular activities and put strong emphasis on critical thinking.
What both systems share, however, is a commitment to reducing inequality. In each country, the government works to ensure that a child in a poor area receives the same quality of teaching as one in a wealthy area. This, researchers suggest, may be more important than any particular syllabus. Systems that allow large gaps between schools tend to have more dropouts and lower average results.
